Python Lab

From one thermometer reading to judging a measurement

Learn data analysis with Python in eight small steps, right here in the browser. A cup of tea is cooling. Nothing to install.

A cup of tea is cooling on your desk. In eight small steps you will go from one thermometer reading to judging a real measurement. About 45 minutes. Skip what you already know.

1One reading 2Many readings 3See it 4Wobble 5Fit 6Judge 7Repeat 8Noise

1One reading

I know this → skip

The thermometer shows a number. Let's give it a name.

Change the number. Press Run Code.

Your turn

Fill in the blank (___). Press Run Code.

Stuck? Show the answer 
gap = T - room

Now you can store a measurement in a variable and calculate with it.

One reading says nothing about cooling. We need many.

2 · Many readings

2Many readings

I know this → skip

Every 15 seconds, one more reading. A row of numbers with one name is an array.

Change a reading. Press Run Code.

Your turn

Fill in the blank. Press Run Code.

Stuck? Show the answer 
drop = T[0] - T[-1]

Now you can keep many readings in an array and ask it questions.

Numbers in a row are hard to read. Let's look at them.

3 · See it

3See it

I know this → skip

Our eyes read a picture faster than a column of numbers.

Change the marker. Press Run Code.

Your turn

Fill in both blanks. Press Run Code.

Stuck? Show the answer 
plt.plot(t[:10], T[:10], "o")

Now you can turn numbers into a graph with labelled axes, and cut out the part you want.

The points are not exactly on a curve. Each reading wobbles. By how much?

4 · Wobble

4Wobble

I know this → skip

Read the same temperature twice and you get two numbers. The typical gap between them is σ (sigma).

Drag the slider. The bars on the points are ±σ.

viewof noise = Inputs.range([0.05, 3], {value: 0.4, step: 0.05, label: "wobble σ (°C)"})

How much one reading can be off, in °C. Here every point has a bar of ± σ. More wobble: messier points.

Your turn

Fill in the blank. Press Run Code, then again: every run is a new set of readings.

Stuck? Show the answer 
sigma = T.std()

Now you can measure the wobble of a reading: σ is the standard deviation of repeated readings.

Now we know how much the points wobble. Which curve passes through them?

5 · Fit

5Fit

I know this → skip

Newton: the gap between tea and room shrinks by the same fraction every second. Python finds the one number that matters: τ.

Drag the slider: the fit follows. Then read the code.

viewof cooling_time = Inputs.range([60, 400], {value: 240, step: 10, label: "cooling time τ (s)"})

How slowly the tea cools: after τ seconds the gap to room temperature has shrunk to about 37%. Larger τ means slower cooling. This is the number the fit has to find.

The same thing in code

Change a number. Press Run Code.

Your turn

Use the fit to predict. Fill in the blank (use np.log). Press Run Code.

Stuck? Show the answer 
t60 = -tau * np.log((60 - Ta) / (T0 - Ta))

Now you can fit a law to data, read τ with its uncertainty, and use it to predict.

A fit always returns numbers, even for a wrong law. How do you know it is good?

6 · Judge

6Judge

I know this → skip

The residuals (data − fit) and χ² tell you whether to believe a fit.

Change the word in quotes. Press Run Code. Watch the light.

Your turn

Compute the number behind the light. Fill in the blank. Press Run Code.

Stuck? Show the answer 
chi2 = np.sum(residuals ** 2)

Now you can tell a good fit from a bad one: the residuals look like noise and the reduced χ² is about 1 (green).

The fit looks good. But is the ± it reports honest? Repeat the experiment and see.

7 · Repeat

7Repeat

I know this → skip

Do the experiment again, and again. If the fit's ± is honest, τ scatters by about that much. Real noise often has memory: each reading remembers the one before.

Same experiment, again and again. Change a number in the code. Press Run Code.

Challenge. Which memory makes the fit overconfident by a factor 2? The fit gets τ right on average. What does it get wrong?

Now you can check whether a fit's uncertainty is honest by repeating the experiment on the computer (a Monte Carlo).

Memory fools the fit. How does it look inside real data?

8 · Noise

8Noise

I know this → skip

Noise is not only how much. It can have memory. Look at the residuals, then at your own data.

Drag the sliders. The chip is the memory of the noise.

viewof memory = Inputs.range([0, 0.95], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "memory"})

How much each noise value remembers the one before. 0: every reading is independent (white noise). Near 1: the noise wanders slowly. The spread of the values stays the same; only the order changes.

viewof thermo_step = Inputs.range([0, 0.5], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "thermometer step (°C)"})

A digital thermometer shows steps, not every value. With a big step the histogram turns into teeth; the rounding alone adds a wobble of about step/√12.

Your turn

Your data. A cooling measurement is below. Press Run Code; then paste your own (time, temperature) lines in place of it.

If the chip is amber or red, the wobble of your data has memory: the ± of the fit is too optimistic.

Now you can read the noise in real data: how much it wobbles, whether it has memory, and what that does to the uncertainty.

That is the whole path.

The end

Where you are now

  1. Store a measurement in a variable and calculate with it.
  2. Keep many readings in an array and ask it questions.
  3. Turn numbers into a graph with labelled axes.
  4. Measure the wobble σ of a reading.
  5. Fit a law, read τ ± its uncertainty, and predict with it.
  6. Judge a fit with the residuals and the reduced χ².
  7. Repeat an experiment on the computer to test the uncertainty.
  8. Read the noise in real data: wobble and memory.

Want to go deeper? Play with the noise itself: its memory, the thermometer step, and how much averaging really helps.

Noise Lab →
NoteWords
  • variable: a name for a value, like T = 78.3.
  • array: many values in a row, with one name.
  • σ (sigma), noise, wobble: how much one reading can be off. The bars on the points.
  • fit: finding the numbers that bring a curve closest to the data.
  • cooling time (τ, tau): how fast the tea cools. Larger means slower.
  • residual: data minus fit, point by point.
  • χ² (chi-squared): around 1 (green) the fit agrees with the bars; higher (amber, red) something is off.
  • memory (autocorrelation): how much a noise value resembles the one before.
  • repeat (Monte Carlo): do the experiment many times on the computer and look at the scatter of the result.
  • function, lambda, dictionary: a recipe with inputs; a tiny unnamed recipe; a labelled collection like laws["newton"].
NoteAbout this page

Python runs inside your browser (Pyodide, WebAssembly): nothing you type is sent to a server. The first visit downloads tens of MB of Python files and page libraries from a public content delivery network (jsDelivr), which can see your IP address; later visits use the browser cache. The data are simulated.
